results.title:
AI Supply-Chain Pentesting: Attacking Models through Training, Updates, and Dependencies
(Hacking AI without Touching Production Systems.)
results.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems become embedded in critical decision-making workflows, security research has largely focused on defending models at runtime. Attention has centered on prompt injection, inference-time abuse, and output manipulation, implicitly assuming that models arrive in production as trustworthy artifacts. This assumption is increasingly fragile. Modern AI systems are assembled through complex and opaque supply chains involving datasets, pre-trained models, fine-tuning pipelines, dependency ecosystems, and automated update mechanisms. Each stage introduces opportunities for adversarial influence that remain largely unexplored by conventional security testing. This paper examines AI security from a supply-chain perspective, arguing that many impactful compromises occur upstream, long before models are deployed into production environments. We introduce the concept of AI supply-chain pentesting as a systematic approach to identifying and evaluating vulnerabilities introduced during training, updating, and dependency integration. Unlike traditional pentesting, which probes live systems for exploitable behaviours, supply-chain pentesting focuses on how model behaviour can be shaped, biased, or backdoored through manipulation of data sources, model reuse practices, update channels, and third-party components. The paper analyzes key attack surfaces across the AI lifecycle, including data poisoning, pre-trained model reuse, automated finetuning workflows, and continuous model updates. Through realistic threat modeling and scenario-driven analysis, we demonstrate how adversaries can influence model behaviour without directly interacting with production systems. These attacks are often stealthy, durable, and difficult to detect through runtime monitoring, as malicious behaviour may only manifest under rare or context-specific conditions. We further argue that existing security methodologies are poorly suited to detect supplychain compromises in AI systems. Traditional defenses assume static code, clear trust boundaries, and observable failures. In contrast, AI models internalize patterns from their inputs, allowing compromised upstream components to persist across deployments and versions. Addressing these risks requires rethinking AI security as a lifecycle problem rather than a deployment problem. By framing the AI supply chain as a primary attack surface, this work highlights a critical gap in current AI security practice and proposes a foundation for developing more robust, adversarially informed testing methodologies. The findings underscore the need for greater scrutiny of training pipelines, update mechanisms, and dependency ecosystems as AI systems continue to proliferate across high-stakes domains.

results.title: AI and Automation in Cyber Defense
results.abstract: The rapid digitization of the food production industry has led to an increased reliance on smart technologies, IoT-enabled systems, and automated supply chains. While these advancements enhance productivity and efficiency, they also expose critical infrastructure to evolving cybersecurity threats. This book chapter explores the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and automation in fortifying cyber defense mechanisms tailored for the food production sector. AI-powered threat detection, predictive analytics, and automated incident response systems are redefining traditional security strategies, enabling proactive threat mitigation. The chapter delves into key areas such as machine learning-driven anomaly detection, blockchain-based food traceability, real-time network monitoring, and cybersecurity compliance frameworks.

results.title: Internal and External Dependencies
AI-Driven Payment Solutions for the Global Food Supply Chain
results.abstract: The global food supply chain faces increasing complexities due to inefficiencies, fraud, and payment delays. AI-driven payment solutions offer a transformative approach by integrating machine learning, blockchain, and smart contracts to enhance transaction transparency, security, and efficiency. These solutions enable real-time payments, reduce intermediaries, and mitigate financial risks for stakeholders, including farmers, distributors, and retailers. This chapter explores the role of AI in revolutionizing payment mechanisms, addressing challenges such as cross-border transactions, currency fluctuations, and fraud detection. Case studies and real-world implementations demonstrate how AI-powered financial technologies contribute to a more resilient and sustainable food supply chain.

results.title: Autonomous Multi-Agent AI Architecture for National-Scale Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Management: Design, Deployment, and Outcomes
results.venue: The American Journal of Engineering and Technology
results.abstract: Pharmaceutical supply chains represent one of the most operationally demanding environments for artificial intelligence deployment, requiring continuous demand forecasting, expiration tracking, procurement automation, and multi-location coordination under conditions that permit minimal margin for error. This paper presents the design, implementation, and real-world deployment outcomes of Restocks AI, an autonomous multi-agent AI platform engineered to replace manual pharmaceutical supply chain operations at national scale. The system integrates predictive inventory engines, multi-agent decisioning frameworks, distributed task-processing infrastructure, and real-time data pipelines to autonomously manage end-to-end supply chain operations across geographically dispersed pharmacy networks. The platform was deployed across two pharmaceutical organizations in Uzbekistan spanning a combined 427 pharmacy locations across all 14 administrative regions, including one of the country's largest private pharmacy networks (150+ locations) and the largest government-operated pharmaceutical institution (277 locations). Deployment results demonstrated 70% reduction in manual operational workload, 30% acceleration of replenishment cycles, 65% reduction in pharmaceutical expiration waste, 70% reduction in stockout incidents, and a combined financial impact of 812 billion Uzbek sum. These results demonstrate that autonomous multi-agent AI systems can effectively manage pharmaceutical supply chains at national scale, offering a replicable architecture with significant implications for healthcare infrastructure, public health outcomes, and the broader application of multi-agent AI in critical industries.

results.title: AI Cybersecurity in an Automotive Manufacturing Supply Chain: Security Challenges and Solutions
results.abstract: The automotive industry's growing reliance on artificial intelligence (AI) couples software, data, and digital decision systems with globally distributed physical supply chains. From supplier quality records and computer-vision inspection to manufacturing execution systems and production scheduling, failures in shared AI dependencies can propagate into line stoppages, defective components, recalls, and vehicle safety risks. This article examines these exposures through four structural AI supply chain cybersecurity gaps: checkability, versioning, transparency, and provenance. Checkability concerns whether externally developed models and their training processes can be independently verified; versioning addresses compatibility among models, cameras, preprocessing, firmware, and component revisions; transparency concerns silent deterioration despite healthy operational dashboards; and provenance addresses tracing AI decisions to supplier lots and individual vehicles. To mitigate these risks, the article proposes signed training attestations, independent model validation, configuration lockfiles, controlled deployment, artifact-aware behavioral monitoring, and bidirectional lineage linking AI artifacts with manufacturing events and vehicle identification numbers. Together, these measures provide a framework for improving accountability, production resilience, recall preparedness, and passenger safety across interconnected automotive AI supply chains.

results.title: Supply Chain, Energy, and AI Nexus: Evaluating AI Energy Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
SkillFortify: Formal Analysis and Supply Chain Security for Agentic AI Skills
results.abstract: The rapid proliferation of agentic AI skill ecosystems-exemplified by OpenClaw (228,000 GitHub stars) and Anthropic Agent Skills (75,600 stars)-has introduced a critical supply chain attack surface. The ClawHavoc campaign (January-February 2026) infiltrated over 1,200 malicious skills into the OpenClaw marketplace, while Mal-Tool catalogued 6,487 malicious tools that evade conventional detection. In response, twelve reactive security tools emerged, yet all rely on heuristic methods that provide no formal guarantees. We present SkillFortify, the first formal analysis framework for agent skill supply chains, with six contributions: (1) the DY-Skill attacker model, a Dolev-Yao adaptation to the five-phase skill lifecycle with a maximality proof; (2) a sound static analysis framework grounded in abstract interpretation; (3) capability-based sandboxing with a confinement proof; (4) an Agent Dependency Graph with SAT-based resolution and lockfile semantics; (5) a trust score algebra with formal monotonicity; and (6) SKillFoRtifyBench, a 540-skill benchmark. SkillFortify achieves 96.95% F1 (95% CI: [95.1%, 98.4%]) with 100% precision and 0% false positive rate on 540 skills, while SAT-based resolution handles 1,000-node graphs in under 100 ms.

results.title: Governing Autonomous Enterprises: A Transaction Cost Perspective on Multi-Agent AI Systems in Supply Chain Operations
results.abstract: Abstract Problem definition : The rapid proliferation of autonomous multi-agent AI systems (MAS) in enterprise environments creates novel governance challenges that existing business frameworks have not addressed. Relevance : As organizations deploy agent-to-agent transaction networks across B2B supply chain operations, the absence of theoretically grounded governance models exposes firms to systemic algorithmic risk, cascade failures, and runaway operational costs. Methodology : Anchored in Transaction Cost Economics (TCE), this paper identifies three novel algorithmic transaction cost dimensions—semantic blind spots, black-box drift, and log decryption costs—and applies Design Science Research (DSR) principles to instantiate a computational governance artifact. Results : The proposed Three-Layered Governance Framework, comprising Deterministic Financial Guardrails, Semantic Communication Logs, and Dynamic Human-in-the-Loop Triggers, demonstrably prevents cascade failures across four simulated supply shock scenarios, preserving up to $40,000 in operational capital per autonomous transaction loop. Managerial implications : Supply chain executives and enterprise architects can deploy this modular, layer-by-layer governance model to safely scale autonomous procurement agents without sacrificing operational velocity or corporate accountability.

results.title: Supply chain security and global dependencies in the trade of phosphorus-related products
Modernizing the Food Industry
Leveraging AI for Real-Time Inventory Management in Perishable Goods Supply Chains
results.abstract: Managing inventory in perishable goods supply chains presents unique challenges due to fluctuating demand, short shelf life, and the risk of spoilage. Traditional inventory management systems often struggle to maintain optimal stock levels while minimizing waste and ensuring product freshness. This chapter explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming real-time inventory management in perishable goods supply chains. AI-driven forecasting models leverage machine learning and predictive analytics to enhance demand forecasting, automate replenishment, and optimize storage conditions. Computer vision and IoT-enabled sensors further contribute by monitoring product quality and providing real-time data for decision-making. Additionally, AI-powered automation and robotics streamline warehouse operations, reducing human errors and increasing efficiency.

results.title: V.E.T. — Vendor Entity Threat Detection: An AI-Powered Data Fusion Framework for U.S. Supply Chain Security
results.abstract: This paper introduces V.E.T. (Vendor Entity Threat Detection), an AI-powered data fusion framework designed to identify high-risk entities — including shell companies, sanctions-listed organizations, and adversarial front companies — embedded within U.S. commercial and government procurement supply chains. The V.E.T. system addresses a documented gap in existing vendor vetting methodologies, which rely predominantly on manual review, siloed databases, and reactive auditing processes inadequate against sophisticated threat actors employing complex corporate structuring techniques. V.E.T. proposes a multi-layer machine learning architecture that cross-references six primary data domains: corporate registry records, beneficial ownership disclosures, financial transaction patterns, logistics and shipping data, sanctions list databases (OFAC, BIS Entity List, CAATSA), and open-source intelligence (OSINT) feeds. The target performance threshold is a precision above 85% on high-risk vendor classification, validated against a curated benchmark dataset. The framework is aligned with requirements established under Executive Order 13873, NSPM-33, and NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 governing supply chain risk management in U.S. government and critical infrastructure contexts. The paper presents the system architecture, data integration design, risk-scoring methodology, and a phased proof-of-concept implementation plan. V.E.T. is built as a shared service accessible through standard API integration, suitable for adoption by federal procurement agencies, financial institutions, and critical infrastructure operators without dependency on any single vendor or employer.

results.title: Cybersecurity Risks in AI-Agent-Supported Supply-Chain Systems Across Multi-Cloud Environments: A Literature Review and Analytical Synthesis
results.abstract: This structured integrative review examines cybersecurity risks that arise when AI agents support operational supply-chain decisions through machine-learning models and data in distributed multi-cloud environments. The review brings together five related research streams: AI agents in operational supply chains; security of AI agents; machine-learning and data integrity; multi-cloud security and identity; and cybersecurity risk management in supply chains. The reviewed literature shows that these streams are established to different degrees. Combined, these streams point to several supply-chain-relevant risk conditions, supported by direct supply-chain evidence for some and transferred evidence for others: manipulated demand forecasts that can resemble a genuine demand shock; delegated non-human identities that can complicate decision provenance (a derived concern); exposure of procurement and negotiation agents to manipulation; operational consequences that differ by supply-chain function; and multi-cloud deployment as a condition that adds identity, API, configuration, policy, and telemetry boundaries. An initial coding of 12 studies in which AI agents perform or support operational supply-chain tasks found seven with no substantive security treatment, three with security mentioned in passing, one with qualitative security discussion, and one with dedicated conceptual threat analysis; none reported an empirical security evaluation or addressed multi-cloud deployment. This result does not indicate that security research is absent; the documented literature instead shows limited integration across agent security, ML/data integrity, multi-cloud identity, and operational supply-chain consequences, and direct empirical evidence for a complete cross-layer relationship remains sparse. The review distinguishes reported findings from derived connections and unsupported links, and it reports database and access limitations explicitly.

results.title: Securing AI-Powered Food Systems Strategies and Solutions
results.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in food systems has revolutionized agriculture, supply chains, and food security. However, it also introduces critical security challenges, including data vulnerabilities, cyber threats, and ethical concerns. This chapter explores the strategies and solutions necessary to secure AI-powered food systems, focusing on data privacy, cybersecurity frameworks, AI governance, and risk mitigation techniques. By addressing potential threats and implementing robust security measures, stakeholders can ensure the resilience and integrity of AI-driven food ecosystems. This chapter also highlights case studies and best practices that demonstrate successful implementations of secure AI applications in the food industry.

results.title: The Role of AI in Next-Generation BI Innovations in Data Processing and Visualization for Food Chain Management
results.abstract: The food production industry is undergoing a digital transformation, leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) to enhance business intelligence (BI) processes. Traditional BI systems struggle with processing vast amounts of data generated from IoT devices, supply chains, and consumer interactions. AI-driven BI solutions offer real-time analytics, predictive insights, and automated decision-making, revolutionizing food production management. This chapter explores the role of AI in optimizing data collection, processing, and visualization in food production. It discusses machine learning algorithms for pattern recognition, AI-powered data visualization for actionable insights, and natural language processing (NLP) for intuitive reporting. Case studies highlight improvements in operational efficiency, waste reduction, and supply chain optimization through AI-driven BI. Additionally, the chapter examines challenges such as data security, integration complexities, and ethical concerns.

results.title: Developing AI-Enabled Early Detection Systems for Supply Chain Failure to Strengthen U.S. Critical Infrastructure Security and National Resilience
results.abstract:
Background: U.S. critical infrastructure depends on deep, multi-tier supply networks whose failures propagate across sectors, yet federal risk management for these networks remains largely periodic and retrospective. Machine learning has been applied to supplier-level disruption prediction and network economics has documented how shocks propagate, but little work evaluates, under an explicit false-alert cost, whether early-warning systems that exploit supply-network structure give critical-service operators more lead time than monitoring of immediate suppliers.
Objective: To develop a conceptual framework for AI-enabled early detection of supply chain failure in critical infrastructure, to state it as four testable propositions, and to examine those propositions in a transparent, fully synthetic proof-of-concept.
Methods: We synthesized peer-reviewed literature and U.S. policy documents (1997-2026) on supply chain resilience, production-network propagation, machine-learning disruption prediction, anomaly detection, and critical infrastructure policy. We then built a fictional five-tier, four-sector, 120-node dependency network (KIRC) with simulated weekly signals, disruption events with precursors, and lagged propagation, and compared five detectors at matched false-alert budgets across 40 replicate synthetic worlds: a tier-1 threshold monitor (A), a multi-tier Isolation Forest (B), a propagation-aware graph detector (C), and two supervised gradient-boosting detectors trained on separate labeled worlds (D1 without and D2 with graph-exposure features). Sensitivity analyses varied noise, cross-sector coupling, event frequency, dependency-map completeness, visibility depth, link delays, precursor length, the propagation rule, and signal withholding and injection; thresholds were also set from held-out calibration worlds.
Results: In the synthetic worlds, the graph detector discriminated impending critical-node failures better than the tier-1 monitor (AUC 0.75 versus 0.59; paired difference +0.158, 95% bootstrap interval 0.150 to 0.166, in all 40 worlds). At a budget of ten false-alert episodes per world, event-level recall was 0.31 for C and 0.31 for B versus 0.21 for A, and mean warning lead time was 1.27, 1.31 and 0.89 weeks; the paired differences between C and B on these metrics included zero. Most failure onsets went unwarned by every unsupervised detector (69-79%). The discrimination advantage of C narrowed from +0.15 to +0.05 AUC with 40% of dependency edges missing and to +0.02 with 60% missing, and did not grow with cross-sector coupling. The supervised detectors warned far more: recall 0.68 (D1) and 0.89 (D2) with mean lead times of 3.0 and 6.6 weeks, and graph-exposure features added to supervised performance (D2 over D1: +0.21 recall, +3.6 weeks); but they were trained on worlds generated by the same process as the test worlds. Fixed thresholds from held-out worlds changed conclusions little. Because propagation and precursors were built into the data-generating process, all results are illustrative only.
Conclusions: The framework identifies multi-tier visibility, dependency-map completeness, labeled incident history, and false-alert budgeting as the design choices on which early-warning value depends, and it yields falsifiable propositions for testing against real supplier, logistics, and infrastructure data. The proof-of-concept offers no evidence that any real system would perform as simulated; it demonstrates the logic, the evaluation protocol, and the conditions under which the expected advantage erodes.

results.title: Secure AI Model Training in Manufacturing R&D: Confidential Computing, Model Watermarking, and Supply Chain Security Controls
A supply chain analytics framework for selective supplier rewiring using agent-based network simulation
AI-Powered Transformation
results.abstract: This chapter explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Workday systems to drive digital transformation within the food industry. Using a real-world case study, it illustrates how AI-enhanced Workday solutions optimize workforce management, streamline operations, and improve decision-making capabilities across food production and supply chains. The chapter delves into specific AI applications such as predictive analytics, talent acquisition automation, and performance management in the context of a leading food company. It further examines the measurable impacts on operational efficiency, employee satisfaction, and compliance. The findings highlight the pivotal role AI plays in redefining HR and financial processes, demonstrating the potential for scalable and sustainable innovation in the food sector.

results.title: AI Supply Chain Security: MBOM-PQC Provenance, PQC Attestation, and a Maturity Model for Quantum-Resistant Assurance
results.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly depend on multi-stage supply chains that incorporate pre-trained models, third-party datasets, open-source libraries, and automated pipelines, creating an expanding attack surface in which model poisoning, dependency compromise, and provenance manipulation can undermine integrity before deployment. Existing AI governance frameworks—including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and Secure Software Development Framework—acknowledge supply chain risks but do not define verifiable model provenance or cryptographically durable integrity guarantees. The transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) compounds this gap: classical digital signatures used to verify model lineage, dataset integrity, and pipeline attestation will become vulnerable to quantum-enabled forgery within the operational lifetime of many AI systems. This paper synthesizes evidence from policy, standards, and incident sources to characterize the AI supply chain threat landscape and the cryptographic dependencies that the PQC transition disrupts. It proposes three integrated design-science artifacts: a Model Bill of Materials with PQC-safe extensions (MBOM-PQC) defining a verifiable provenance schema; a unified signing and attestation pipeline integrating ML-DSA and hybrid signature modes; and a five-level Supply Chain Assurance Maturity Model (SCAMM) for repeatable organizational evaluation. These contributions provide a structured foundation for AI supply chain integrity in cloud-connected, mission-critical smart systems, ensuring verifiable lineage, authenticity, and trustworthiness through the PQC transition. Empirical validation is deferred to future work.

results.title: Malicious AI Models Undermine Software Supply-Chain Security
results.abstract: Unveiling the dark side.

results.title: Mapping Material Dependencies and Supply Chain Exposure: A Regional Vulnerability Assessment in France
Resource-Optimized and Energy-Aware Agentic AI Framework Anchored on Blockchain for Secure Software Supply Chains
results.abstract: This paper proposes a blockchain-backed agentic security framework designed to safeguard the complete software development lifecycle (SDLC) while also securing the agentic AI components responsible for monitoring it. The framework coordinates a set of specialised security agents, covering source integrity, dependency and SBOM analysis, CI configura tion auditing, artifact verification, and runtime policy evaluation, each supported by a large language model (LLM) that interprets artefacts, reasons over tool outputs, and produces structured security reports. To ensure agent trustworthiness, every agent generates a cryptographically signed attestation that is recorded in a permissioned blockchain via smart contracts, including an agent registry, an immutable attestation log, and an enforceable release-policy module. Communication among agents and with blockchain nodes is secured using a consortium-operated certificate authority, ensuring authenticated and tamper-resistant interactions. A detailed use-case and sequence flow demonstrate how a source code security agent performs analysis, anchors its attestation on-chain, and triggers a verifiable allow/block deployment decision. The proposed framework of fers decentralised integrity transparent provenance, uninterrupted security assurance and a generalisable architecture to incorporate the agentic AI into the modern software supply chain security.

results.title: Trustworthy AI LLM Scalability Risk Index (LSRI): A Cybersecurity Framework Assessing Agentic-AI Security & Software Model Supply Chain Safety Boosting AI-Generated Malware Defense & Explainability Mitigating Emerging Risks of Generative AI
results.abstract: As AI shifts from human-in-the-loop interfaces to autonomous multi-agent systems capable of real-time code execution and tool integration through protocols like the Model Context Protocol (MCP), traditional SAST, DAST, and legacy AI safety methods fail to detect modern agentic-AI threats. This paper introduces the LLM Scalability Risk Index (LSRI), a parametric framework and cybersecurity standard for stress-testing autonomous orchestration pipelines. LSRI measures the operational thresholds where load, compounding hallucinations, data poisoning, and adversarial prompt injections including jailbreaking and indirect prompt injection cause security boundaries to fail. Beyond RLHF and RLAIF, we present a Verifiable Root of Trust architecture using cryptographic attestation, semantic policy enforcement, and continuous runtime verification to secure the AI software supply chain. LSRI defends against malicious LoRA adapters, weight tampering, dependency typosquatting, and unsafe model artifacts from public registries such as Hugging Face and GitHub. By replacing post-hoc alignment with verifiable runtime controls, LSRI provides scalable API defense, safer agentic orchestration under heavy cloud workloads, stronger polymorphic malware detection, automated red-teaming, and improved system explainability. Aligned with NIST AI RMF, OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, and ISO 42001, LSRI establishes a deployable compliance baseline for securing generative AI ecosystems including ChatGPT, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Copilot, LLaMA, Gemini, and Bedrock. LSRI also supports capital market risk analysis by reducing exposure across technology portfolios linked to indices such as NASDAQ-100, QQQ, and semiconductor-driven supply chains.

results.title: Scanning the Harness: Configuration Exposures in AI Coding-Agent Supply Chains
results.abstract: AI coding agents rely on repository instructions, skills, hooks, tool-server declarations, and subagent definitions. These artifacts distribute both behavior and access to executable dependencies, making configuration review part of the agent software supply chain. We study 3,171 public GitHub repositories: 2,660 assembled setups and 511 skill collections. Deterministic analysis, mechanical re-derivation, model-assisted adjudication, human review, and platform documentation checks identify six categories of configuration exposure and conformance issues. Unpinned MCP package declarations occur in 9.8% of setups, broad execution grants in 2.5%, and broad skill tool preapproval in 3.8%. Their union covers 409 setups (15.4%); among setups with MCP configuration, 24.5% contain an unpinned declaration. Including required-field and skill-format issues brings the setup rate to 17.9% and the collection rate to 6.8%. Holding the six categories fixed, contextual review changes the setup rate from 18.3% to 17.9%; rule selection explains most of the reduction from the broader candidate set. The findings identify concrete opportunities to pin dependencies, review execution pre approval, and check component conformance before distribution or use. A documented permission exception also exposes a shared error in the scanner and its mechanical audit, motivating version-specific semantic checks. The study provides reproducible evidence about repository declarations; agreement with human judgments informs label validation, while runtime consequences and recall remain unmeasured.

results.title: SOK: A Taxonomy of Attack Vectors and Defense Strategies for Agentic Supply Chain Runtime
results.abstract: Agentic systems based on large language models (LLMs) operate not merely as text generators but as autonomous entities that dynamically retrieve information and invoke tools. This execution model shifts the attack surface from traditional build-time artifacts to inference-time dependencies, exposing agents to manipulation through untrusted data and probabilistic capability resolution. While prior work has examined model-level vulnerabilities, security risks arising from the complex, cyclic runtime behavior of agents remain fragmented. This paper systematizes existing research into a unified runtime framework. We categorize threats into data supply chain attacks (distinguishing between transient context injection and persistent memory poisoning) and tool supply chain attacks (spanning discovery, implementation, and invocation phases). Crucially, we identify the emergence of the Viral Agent Loop, where agents effectively become vectors for self-propagating generative worms that require no code vulnerabilities to spread. We argue for a transition to a Zero-Trust Runtime Architecture, where context is treated as untrusted control flow, and tool execution is bounded by cryptographic provenance rather than semantic likelihood.

results.title: Setup Complete, Now You Are Compromised: Weaponizing Setup Instructions Against AI Coding Agents
results.abstract: AI coding agents set up projects by reading documentation and installing the dependencies it lists, without verifying their names, sources, or known vulnerabilities. By editing only a README, requirements file, or Makefile, an attacker can redirect the agent to an untrusted registry, a known-vulnerable version, or a wrong-but-plausible name: documentation becomes a vector for code execution. We present the first systematic evaluation of package-install-time supply-chain attacks delivered through ordinary project-setup documentation across production coding-agent harnesses, probing frontier models on twelve scenarios in five attack classes, grounded in documented incidents. The same model catches an attack through one harness and installs it through another: install-time security rests on the harness-model combination, not the model alone. Agents catch blatant typosquats reliably, but plausible separator-confusion names (azurecore for azure-core) slip through, and how often depends on the harness-model pairing. Source-based attacks like registry redirection are missed almost everywhere. The source blind spot recurs on npm and Cargo, where nearly every model installs the untrusted dependency; name detection carries over less consistently across ecosystems. Security-oriented prompts recover part of the gap but only for the dimension they name; a deterministic pre-install check that verifies names, sources, and versions before any code runs closes most of it.

results.title: Human-Certified Module Repositories for the AI Age
results.abstract: Human-Certified Module Repositories (HCMRs) are introduced in this work as a new architectural model for constructing trustworthy software in the era of AI-assisted development. As large language models increasingly participate in code generation, configuration synthesis, and multi-component integration, the reliability of AI-assembled systems will depend critically on the trustworthiness of the building blocks they use. Today's software supply-chain incidents and modular development ecosystems highlight the risks of relying on components with unclear provenance, insufficient review, or unpredictable composition behavior. We argue that future AI-driven development workflows require repositories of reusable modules that are curated, security-reviewed, provenance-rich, and equipped with explicit interface contracts. To this end, we propose HCMRs, a framework that blends human oversight with automated analysis to certify modules and support safe, predictable assembly by both humans and AI agents. We present a reference architecture for HCMRs, outline a certification and provenance workflow, analyze threat surfaces relevant to modular ecosystems, and extract lessons from recent failures. We further discuss implications for governance, scalability, and AI accountability, positioning HCMRs as a foundational substrate for reliable and auditable AI-constructed software systems.

results.title: Agentic process evidence
results.abstract: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations

results.title: MalSkillBench: A Runtime-Verified Benchmark of Malicious Agent Skills
results.abstract: AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Gemini CLI increasingly extend themselves with third-party skills: markdown packages bundling natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and tool permissions. Because a skill is at once code and agent-facing instruction, it introduces a supply chain dependency whose risk is neither pure code nor pure prompt. Detection tools have never been measured against verified ground truth spanning this hybrid space, leaving their effectiveness unknown and wild-only evaluations biased. We present MalSkillBench, the first runtime-verified benchmark of malicious agent skills: 3,944 malicious skills labeled along a three-dimensional taxonomy of 108 cells. Of these, 3,214 come from a closed-loop Generate-Verify-Feedback pipeline admitting only samples whose malicious behavior fires inside a Docker sandbox under system-call monitoring and an LLM judge; we add 703 in-the-wild and 4,000 matched benign skills. Our measurements are consistent: code injection reaches 94.5% verification yield but prompt injection only 75.8%, the same fragility that later makes it hard to detect; the wild sample is narrow, dominated by one cryptocurrency-theft campaign (86.6% one behavior, 81% from two accounts) with a small but architecturally new tail attacking the agent control plane; the strongest skill-specific detector reaches 98.4% recall on code injection yet collapses on prompt-injection and agent-control attacks, and wild-only scoring swings the ranking by up to 66 recall points; supply-chain scanners and prompt-injection defenses each see only half of a skill, and no combination recovers the code-instruction relationship. Detecting malicious skills therefore requires reasoning jointly over task intent, code, and instructions. We release the dataset, pipeline, baselines, and results.
